A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PhishBencher and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A-C. The retained material and substantive additions can be reliably matched across versions.

before.justification: v2 reports original contamination experiments, benchmark-tracking evaluations, pretraining and model-merging studies, reverse-engineering results, and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v5 retains original empirical results and adds detector comparisons, benchmark evaluations, and expanded reverse-engineering experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3.4 adds an optional auditor for partial contamination, requiring original model responses and private ground-truth labels. It tests whether randomized answers are correct unusually often when original answers are wrong. This substantially extends v2's proposed Bayes-ceiling detector; the underlying randomization mechanism remains.

E1.justification: v5 adds MATH-500 and HumanEval, extending evaluated data coverage to additional challenging mathematics and Python code completion. Existing benchmarks and languages remain. HumanEval uses the disclosure-allowed strategy described in Appendix B.1.

E2.justification: The canary-string comparisons are retained, while v5 evaluates Min-k% and Min-k%++ across six benchmarks and multilingual MMLU-ProX in Figure 7. v2 cited the Min-k% work but did not evaluate these detectors.

E3.justification: New detector experiments introduce seen/unseen splits, training on the seen subset, question-only detector inputs, and AUC evaluation. HumanEval combines unit-test success with randomized-comment checking. Reverse-engineering evaluations add candidate-verification and code-completion procedures, plus 25% and 10% Bayes-accuracy settings.

E4.justification: v2's reverse-engineering strategy is retained as P1. v5 adds candidate verification (P2), code recovery (P3), sensitivity to lower Bayes accuracies in Table 10, and a MathQA failure case in Table 11. Existing reasoning, prompt-variation, and randomization ablations remain.

E5.justification: Both versions retain three-seed mean/standard-deviation reporting and 5% binomial tests. Section 3.4 newly proposes memorization/chance estimators and a t-test for zero excess memorization, substantially extending the statistical procedures. No corresponding empirical auditor-test results are reported.

E6.justification: Table 3 revises existing results: HLE-MC reverse-engineering/P1 accuracy changes from 15.23% to 29.17%, and original-prompt accuracy from 7.77% to 18.25%; P2 adds 58.66%. New detector, benchmark, and attack-sensitivity results are reported. Table 6 changes aggregate Kendall's tau from 0.96 to 0.93 with expanded coverage. These revisions do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: Theorems 1-2 and their proofs are retained. v5 adds Theorem 3, memorization/chance definitions and estimators, a contamination-fraction condition, and Appendix A.3's proof. The new population chance statistic and its claimed unbiased estimator in Equation (5) have inconsistent normalization.

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contribution summary retain the central benchmark-release, progress-tracking, and contamination-detection claims. The conclusion newly includes certain open-ended tasks, such as code generation, within its stated applicability.

C2.justification: v5 adds discussion of contamination below the Bayes ceiling, the auditor's information requirements, complementary use of Min-k detectors, and why candidate verification may fail. It strengthens claims about protecting individual labels. However, its assertion that HLE-MC remains below 50% for both attack prompts contradicts Table 3's P2 result of 58.66%.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds HumanEval comment-checking details and MATH-500/HumanEval sizes and access links. Tables 7-9 expand reusable reverse-engineering templates. These are targeted reproducibility additions; existing hardware disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v5 adds references for Min-k%++, HumanEval, MATH/MATH-500, and Mergenetic, and discusses PhishBencher's relationship to Min-k detectors. The main related-work survey remains largely unchanged. BIG-bench's preprint-to-publication update represents the same cited work.

P1.justification: The method gains numbered subsections, the coin-flipping explanation and baseline discussion move, and reverse-engineering prose is substantially expanded locally. Much of the introduction, retained theoretical explanation, and concluding contribution statement remains unchanged.

P2.justification: v5 adds the Min-k figure and code example, expands benchmark plots, restructures Table 3 into P1/P2/P3/Original columns, and adds attack-template, sensitivity-result, and failure-case tables. Existing figures are largely retained despite renumbering and relocation.

improvement.justification: Compared with v2's canary-only comparisons and single reverse-engineering strategy, v5 provides broader and more informative evaluations. However, the new auditor's chance statistic and estimator are inconsistently normalized, and the robustness discussion contradicts HLE-MC's 58.66% P2 result. These problems undermine the added guarantees and interpretation, leaving the net quality effect uncertain.
